prompt: A sale is rung up at 10:21, stored by Kafka at 14:00 and read by a report next week. Which of its times never changes, however often it is read?

choices.text: The time Kafka stored it, because the log never rewrites a record
choices.why: Ingestion time is fixed too once written, but it is the log's time, not the sale's; send the sale again and it changes.

choices.text: Its event time
choices.why: Right. 10:21 belongs to the sale; the other two belong to the machinery.

choices.text: Its processing time, once the first reader has handled it
choices.why: Processing time is every moment anybody reads it; next week's report gives it another.

choices.text: None of them, since every clock drifts
choices.why: Drift makes a clock wrong, not a recorded time mutable.

prompt: A topic has `message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime`. A producer passes `timestamp=` with 2 March 2026 on a record it sends today. What timestamp does the record carry?

choices.text: 2 March 2026, because the producer set it
choices.why: That is CreateTime's behaviour. LogAppendTime throws the producer's value away.

choices.text: Both, in two fields of the record
choices.why: A record has one timestamp field; the topic decides what goes in it.

choices.text: Today's date, from the clock of the consumer that reads it
choices.why: The consumer's clock is processing time, and it is never written into the record.

choices.text: The broker's clock at the moment it appended the record
choices.why: Right. The console consumer then labels it LogAppendTime.

prompt: With the default `message.timestamp.type`, which is ___, a record keeps whatever timestamp the producer gave it.
`tills.py` sends a sale whose `at` says 2 March, and the consumer prints `CreateTime:` with a number that decodes to the day you ran it. What explains the gap?

choices.text: The broker overwrote the producer's value, as it does on every topic
choices.why: Only a LogAppendTime topic does that, and `clocks` keeps CreateTime.

choices.text: The till's clock is invented; the client stamped the machine's real one
choices.why: Right. `tills.py` sets no timestamp, so the client writes its own present.

choices.text: The consumer converted the time to its own time zone, which moved the date
choices.why: A time zone moves a time by hours, not by seven months.

choices.text: A wrong clock in the virtual machine
choices.why: The machine's clock was right; it was the shop clock that was made up.

prompt: A sale happened at 10:45:00 and reached Kafka at 14:00:00. What is its skew, in minutes?
Why does `late_tills.py` pass `timestamp=` to `produce` instead of leaving it out?

choices.text: Kafka refuses a record with no timestamp
choices.why: A producer that sets none gets its own present stamped by the client.

choices.text: It sends a whole day in seconds, so the present would be wrong
choices.why: Right. It writes the time each sale would have been sent, which a live till gets for free.

choices.text: To make the topic delete each record seven days after its sale, as retention would
choices.why: Retention is the opposite worry: March stamps would be deleted at once, hence retention.ms=-1.

choices.text: So that the console consumer prints the sales in event order
choices.why: The consumer prints in log order whatever the stamps say.

prompt: A delivery company's vans send their scans over the phone network, and the skew plot shows a thin band near the diagonal plus a few rows of points far above it. What are the rows most likely to be?

choices.text: Scans that were made twice
choices.why: A duplicate is a second dot, not a dot moved up; height is the delay.

choices.text: Vans whose clocks run slow
choices.why: A slow clock moves dots consistently by a fixed amount; a flat row means many events arriving at one moment.

choices.text: Vans that lost signal and sent what they held on reconnecting
choices.why: Right. Like Natal's till: many events from a span of time, one arrival time.

choices.text: Scans that arrived before they were made
choices.why: Those would sit below the diagonal, and only a lying clock puts them there.

prompt: In arrival order, five sales have event times 09:00:10, 09:00:40, 09:00:25, 09:01:30, 09:00:50. How far out of order, in seconds, is the last one?
hint: Compare it with the latest event time seen before it.

prompt: In the same five sales, 09:00:10, 09:00:40, 09:00:25, 09:01:30, 09:00:50 in arrival order, how many arrived out of order?
68 of the 360 sales arrived out of order. Why is that not the same as the 38 Natal held back?

choices.text: Thirty were ordinary sales slowed by seconds on the way
choices.why: Right. Slow deliveries from every shop, up to 92 seconds behind.

choices.text: The awk count is wrong, because it compares strings instead of times
choices.why: jq turns each `at` into seconds first; awk compares numbers.

choices.text: Natal's sales were counted twice, once when held and once when sent
choices.why: Each sale is one record, counted once.

choices.text: The other thirty came from a second partition read in parallel
choices.why: The `late` topic has one partition, chosen so that arrival order is one order.

prompt: Why would waiting two minutes before counting fix one group of out-of-order sales and not the other?

choices.text: Two minutes is longer than the slow deliveries and nowhere near Natal's hours
choices.why: Right. The distribution has two populations, and one wait cannot serve both.

choices.text: Natal's sales are in another partition, which no wait can reach
choices.why: They are in the same single partition; the problem is how late they are.

choices.text: Waiting only helps sales from the same shop, because each key keeps a wait of its own
choices.why: The slow deliveries come from every shop, and a wait helps all of them.

choices.text: A wait reorders events by key, and Natal has no key
choices.why: Every sale is keyed by its shop, Natal's included.

prompt: Counted by arrival, the 14:00 hour has 93 sales; by event time, 54. Which number belongs in the manager's report of sales per hour?

choices.text: 93, because those are the sales the system received in that hour
choices.why: That answers a question about the pipeline, not about the shops.
Right. The hour belongs to the sale, and 39 of those 93 happened earlier.

choices.text: Their average, 73.5, to split the difference
choices.why: An average of two answers to two questions answers neither.

choices.text: Neither, until the till in Natal is replaced
choices.why: The till did nothing wrong; it was offline.

prompt: Event times, in arrival order: 10:58, 11:02, 10:59, 11:05, 10:57, 11:10. All arrive between 11:00 and 11:15. Counted by event time, how many fall in the 10:00 hour?
Why does `per_minute.py` use the record's timestamp as processing time instead of its own clock?

choices.text: Reading after the fact, its own clock would put every sale in one minute
choices.why: Right. The record's timestamp is when a reader keeping up would have seen it.

choices.text: Python cannot read the system clock inside a Kafka consumer
choices.why: It can; doing so would just measure the moment of the rerun.

choices.text: The record's timestamp is the event time
choices.why: In `late` it is the time of sending; the event time is `at`.

choices.text: The broker's clock is more accurate than the virtual machine's
choices.why: They are the same machine here; accuracy is not the reason.

prompt: At 11:00, a processor reports the 10:00 hour by event time as 55 sales. At 14:30 it reports the same hour as 62. Which statement is right?

choices.text: The second report is a duplicate count of seven sales
choices.why: Nothing was counted twice; seven sales of that hour had not arrived yet.

choices.text: The processor should have counted by arrival to avoid changing its answer
choices.why: By arrival the answer never changes and is wrong for good.

choices.text: Event-time counts are only final once late events are in
choices.why: Right. The processor cannot know when that is, which is lesson 11's subject.

choices.text: The first report was wrong because the clock in Natal was wrong
choices.why: Natal's clock was right; its sales were late.

prompt: Since Kafka 4.0, what happens by default to a record on a `CreateTime` topic stamped two hours in the future?

choices.text: It is stored, and its timestamp is replaced by the broker's
choices.why: That is what a LogAppendTime topic does.

choices.text: It is stored unchanged, as every timestamp is
choices.why: before Kafka 4.0 that was the default; now the limit is an hour ahead.

choices.text: It is refused
choices.why: Right. `message.timestamp.after.max.ms` is an hour, and the producer gets `Invalid timestamp`.

choices.text: It is stored and moved to the end of the partition
choices.why: A log appends at the end anyway; nothing is moved.

prompt: By default, how many minutes ahead of the broker's clock may a record's timestamp be before a `CreateTime` topic refuses it?
One till's clock is an hour fast. Why is that worse for an event-time pipeline than a till an hour slow?

choices.text: A fast clock's sales are refused by the broker and lost
choices.why: An hour is inside the broker's tolerance, so they are stored.

choices.text: A slow clock is corrected by NTP and a fast one is not, since NTP only moves clocks forward
choices.why: NTP corrects either direction.

choices.text: Its sales push the latest time seen forward, so honest sales look late
choices.why: Right. One fast source moves everybody's sense of time; a slow one only makes its own sales late.

choices.text: Fast clocks make the sales arrive sooner
choices.why: The clock changes the stamp, not the network.

prompt: A sale's `at` is 15:20 and the broker appended it at 15:02. What can a pipeline conclude?

choices.text: The sale is late by eighteen minutes
choices.why: Late means arriving after it happened; this arrived before.

choices.text: The till's clock is wrong, since nothing arrives before it happens
choices.why: Right. Keeping both clocks is what makes this visible.

choices.text: The broker's clock is wrong, since the till is closer to the sale
choices.why: Either could be wrong, but the broker's is the one you run and sync.

choices.text: Kafka will refuse the record, because its event time is later than its arrival
choices.why: Kafka never reads `at`; and eighteen minutes is inside its tolerance anyway.

prompt: Match each question to the clock it should be answered with.

pairs.left: Sales per hour for the manager
Sales the pipeline handles per second
How far behind the consumer is
A card used in two cities ten minutes apart

right_distractors: ingestion time, because it never changes

prompt: When is `LogAppendTime` a reasonable stand-in for event time?

choices.text: When the sources have no clock worth trusting
choices.why: Right. It is stamped by a clock you run, and in a well-behaved stream close to the event.

choices.text: When some sources go offline for hours
choices.why: Then it is hours wrong: Natal's sales were appended at 14:00.

choices.text: When results must be the same in every replay and match event time exactly
choices.why: It is the same in every replay, but it never matches event time exactly.

choices.text: Never: it is processing time under another name
choices.why: Processing time changes with every read; ingestion time is fixed once appended.

prompt: Which of these are costs of counting by event time rather than processing time? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Results are not final at the end of their period
choices.why: Yes: they wait until the processor decides nothing more will come.

choices.text: Open counts are kept as state, per key
choices.why: Yes: an open hour's running count has to live somewhere.

choices.text: Each event needs a trustworthy time inside it
choices.why: Yes: a lying device clock becomes a wrong result.

choices.text: Kafka refuses records whose event time is old
choices.why: Kafka never reads the event time inside the value, and before.max allows any age by default.

choices.text: Replays give different answers
choices.why: That is processing time's flaw; event time gives the same answer every replay.

prompt: `kafka-get-offsets.sh --time` for 13:00 on `late` returns an offset. What does replaying from it give you?

choices.text: Every sale that happened after 13:00, and nothing earlier
choices.why: Natal's morning sales arrived at 14:00, after that offset.

choices.text: Exactly the sales of the 13:00 hour
choices.why: A search finds a starting position, not a set of events, and reading goes on past 14:00.

choices.text: Only the records whose timestamp is after 13:00, skipping the rest
choices.why: A consumer reads every record from the position on; it does not filter by timestamp.

choices.text: Everything that arrived from 13:00 on
choices.why: Right. In `late` the stamp is the time of sending, so the search is by arrival.

prompt: A topic keeps the default seven-day retention, and a producer stamps each record with the sale's event time. A batch of sales from three weeks ago arrives. What happens to them?

choices.text: They are kept for seven days from now
choices.why: Retention is measured with the record's timestamp, not with the time it was written.

choices.text: They are refused by the broker
choices.why: before.max allows any age by default.

choices.text: They are deleted at the next retention check
choices.why: Right, if they are alone in their segment: its newest stamp is already past the limit.

choices.text: They are moved to the start of the partition
choices.why: A log appends; nothing moves to the start.

One of Natal's held sales: put its times in the order they occur.

prompt: Ponto Final wants an alert when a shop sells nothing for an hour. Which design avoids the false alarm of 2 March?

choices.text: Count by event time and alert as soon as an hour has no sales
choices.why: At 11:20 the event-time hour is just as empty: the sales are still in the till.

choices.text: Count by arrival and raise the threshold to two hours
choices.why: Natal was quiet for three hours and forty minutes; the alarm still fires, later.

choices.text: Alert on silence from the till itself, which is a pipeline question, separate from sales per hour
choices.why: Right. Nothing arrived from Natal, which is true and worth knowing; whether it sold is a different question.

choices.text: Switch the topic to LogAppendTime
choices.why: Ingestion time also says 14:00 for Natal's sales.
